newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt group condemns torture, political stagnation.
newsitem.headline: Egypt group condemns torture, political stagnation.

text.p: An Egyptian human rights group said on Monday that 12 inmates died from lack of medical care in prisons and five detainees died from torture in police stations in Egypt in 1996.

The independent Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights said the low-level guerrilla war between militants and police had lost some of its intensity last year but the government used the violence as an excuse to refer dozens of civilians to military court and to illegally detain hundreds more.

"The worst aspect of the crisis of human rights in Egypt remained the ill-treatment and torture of detainees in prisons and police stations," EOHR secretary-general Mohammed Moneib told a news conference to launch the group's annual report.

"There was a relative decrease in the number of acts of violence between security forces and armed Islamic groups. But human rights continued to suffer from the dilemma of the absence of political participation resulting from the government's persistence in monopolising political activity and the use of the emergency law," he said.

Emergency law has been in effect in Egypt since militant army officers assassinated President Anwar Sadat in 1981. Parliament in February approved a presidential decree to extend the law for three more years.
According to EOHR figures, 174 people died in political violence in Egypt in 1996, down from the 373 deaths it recorded in 1995.

Moneib said the group had evidence to show that militant groups were responsible for most violence in 1996, killing policemen, guards and secret agents as well as people they suspected of being police informers.
Militants also continued to kill Christians and tourists in a bid to "undermine the state's stability," EOHR said.
But the group said it also had evidence that security forces used excessive force against militants, killing rather than arresting many of them.

Police in Egypt also illegally detained or randomly arrested hundreds of people after militant attacks, sometimes taking relatives "as hostages to force their wanted relatives to give themselves up", EOHR said.
The Interior Ministry has since 1992 practised a policy of keeping political detainees in prison for years despite court release orders or acquittals, the group added.

"The referral of civilians to military courts continued to be a major concern of the organisation in 1996 given that these courts lack all constitutional and international safeguards for fair trials," Moneib said.

The report said a military court in Egypt tried four cases involving 66 civilians in 1996. The court sentenced 10 of the defendants to death, bringing to 74 the number of people handed execution terms by such courts since December 1992, the year militants launched their bloody campaign to overthrow the government and install a strict Islamic state.
President Hosni Mubarak that year cleared the way for civilians to be tried by the military in an attempt to bypass the lengthy procedures of civilian courts.
Another 10 militant defendants were sentenced to death in 1996 by Supreme State Security Courts, which EOHR said "lack many of the international safeguards for fair trials".

EOHR criticised the government for referring members of the outlawed Moslem Brotherhood -- the largest political Islamic group in Egypt -- to trial in military court in 1996 after they tried to set up a new political party.
A government-appointed committee rejected applications to set up five new political parties in 1996.

"Respecting the right of citizens to establish and join political parties and removing all obstacles to the peaceful and democratic circulation of power are the only means to end violence, which is a natural consequence of the lack of freedom of association and assembly," EOHR said.
EOHR also condemned a decision by the Court of Cassation to uphold a ruling separating an academic from his wife on a claim made by Islamists that his writings had made him an apostate.
The government's spokeswoman on human rights was not immediately available to comment.
